summary: Michigan has no exotic/wild-animal possession permit that captures rodents. The Large Carnivore Act covers only big cats and bears; the roof rat is not on the NREPA Part 413 prohibited/restricted (invasive) list (only nutria and Russian boar are among prohibited mammals); and the Pet Shops Act excludes rodents from its licensing definition. So keeping, breeding, and selling/giving a roof rat is effectively legal/unregulated at the state level. The one concrete requirement is animal-health: importing a non-native rodent needs a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (no Michigan entry permit). Because no rule names the species, it's best labeled unregulated/unclear, and local ordinances may add limits.

kit.problem: In Michigan, keeping, breeding, and rehoming a captive-bred pet roof rat (Rattus rattus) is effectively legal, but no state rule says so by name. The species sits in a gap: it is NOT on Michigan's prohibited or restricted invasive-species list under NREPA Part 413 (the only prohibited mammals are nutria and wild/Russian boar), the Large Carnivore Act covers only big cats and bears, and the Pet Shops Act's definition of "animal" excludes rodents entirely. So no permit captures it and no statute bans it — its lawful status is inferred from silence rather than written down anywhere. That leaves owners, vets, and rescues without a clear document to point to, and it leaves the door open for the species to be wrongly treated as a wild pest. The fix is a written confirmation from the state, not a new law.
kit.ask: Ask MDARD (with DNR for the wildlife-permit point) to confirm IN WRITING that captive-bred domestic roof rats are treated like other unregulated non-native pet rodents: (1) Rattus rattus is not a prohibited or restricted species under NREPA Part 413; (2) no DNR captive-wildlife permit or MDARD exotic-animal permit is required to keep, breed, or rehome them; and (3) the only state movement requirement is an interstate Certificate of Veterinary Inspection on import, with no Michigan entry permit. A short letter, email, or declaratory statement to that effect gives owners and veterinarians something concrete to rely on. It helps to note that being non-native is not, by itself, what makes a species prohibited: the domestic cat and dog are also non-native and are documented to harm native wildlife, yet Michigan permits them because their companionship is judged worth the trade-off — so the relevant question for a few sterile or altered, tame, indoor-only pet rats is the same cost-benefit judgment, which we leave to the state, not the bare fact that the species is non-native.
kit.branch_note: This is an AGENCY / bureaucracy-clarification case, NOT a law-change case. The Michigan law as written already leaves captive-bred roof rats unregulated: the species is absent from the NREPA Part 413 prohibited/restricted lists (only nutria and wild/Russian boar are prohibited mammals — verified), the Large Carnivore Act reaches only big cats and bears, and the Pet Shops Act excludes rodents from "animal." The problem is purely that no rule names the species, so its legal status is inferred from silence and is undocumented — exactly the kind of gap an agency can close with a written clarification or declaratory statement. The correct lever is therefore MDARD's Animal Industry Division (with the DNR confirming the captive-wildlife-permit point), asked to put the existing status in writing. Going to the Legislature here would be the WRONG move and could backfire: there is no defective statute to amend, and opening Part 413 or the exotic-pet statutes invites the species being ADDED to a prohibited list rather than affirmed as a legal pet. Pursue the agency confirmation; do not seek legislation.

template.en:
Subject: Request to confirm in writing the legal status of captive-bred pet roof rats (Rattus rattus)

Dear MDARD Animal Industry Division,

I keep domesticated, captive-bred roof rats (Rattus rattus) as indoor pets. These animals are tame, born in captivity, kept entirely indoors, and never released to the wild. I am writing because Michigan law does not name this species anywhere, which leaves its pet status unclear on paper even though it appears to be unregulated.

From my reading, Rattus rattus is not on the NREPA Part 413 prohibited or restricted species list (only nutria and wild/Russian boar are prohibited mammals), the Large Carnivore Act covers only big cats and bears, and the Pet Shops Act excludes rodents. I am not asking for any change to the law.

I mention one thing only to head off a possible misunderstanding: being a non-native species is not by itself what places an animal on the prohibited list. The domestic cat and dog are also non-native, and are documented to harm native wildlife, yet Michigan permits them because their companionship is judged worth it. I am not asking the state to reach any particular conclusion about my pets — only to confirm where the existing law already places them.

Could you please confirm in writing that: (1) Rattus rattus is not a prohibited or restricted species under Part 413; (2) no DNR captive-wildlife permit or MDARD exotic-animal permit is required to keep, breed, or rehome captive-bred roof rats; and (3) the only state movement requirement is an interstate Certificate of Veterinary Inspection on import, with no Michigan entry permit?

A brief written confirmation would give owners and veterinarians a clear document to rely on. Thank you for your time.

Sincerely,
[Your name]
[Your city, Michigan]
[Your email / phone]

kit.confidence_notes: Verified (June 2026): (1) MDARD's official contact page is live at https://www.michigan.gov/mdard/about/contact-mdard ("Contact MDARD / File a Complaint"), which hosts online forms, lists the general line 800-292-3939, and confirms MDA-Info@Michigan.gov as the after-hours/general department inbox — so both the form page and that email are official. (2) Confirmed across multiple sources (michigan.gov invasives mammals pages; clickondetroit "Michigan's 2 invasive mammals") that the ONLY prohibited mammals under NREPA Part 413 are nutria and wild/Russian boar; Rattus rattus is not listed as prohibited or restricted. (3) Michigan Legislature find/contact pages (legislature.mi.gov) verified but intentionally NOT used as a target, per the branch judgment. The Large Carnivore Act (cats/bears only) and Pet Shops Act (rodents excluded) points come from the prior internal research and statute citations (MCL 287.1101+, MCL 287.331+) and remain consistent with current sources, though I could not re-fetch the legislature PDFs this session (michigan.gov returned 403 to direct fetch; relied on verified search snippets and the grounding file). The DNR Wildlife Permits line (517-284-6210) and the invasive-species program contacts page are from the grounding file; the general michigan.gov/dnr portal and invasives contacts page are stable. Uncertainty: the exact form on the MDARD contact page is a general inquiry/complaint form rather than a dedicated "declaratory ruling" portal, so the agency may route the request internally — phone or the MDA-Info email may get a faster substantive answer. This is a research aid, not legal advice; local city/township/county ordinances may add limits and should be checked separately.

keep.why: No general exotic-possession permit captures rodents. The only exotic-mammal possession ban (Large Carnivore Act, MCL 287.1101+) covers big cats/bears, and R. rattus is not on the NREPA Part 413 prohibited/restricted list (only nutria and Russian boar among prohibited mammals). No statute prohibits or licenses keeping one — but none affirmatively names/exempts the species either, so it's unregulated rather than expressly permitted.
keep.governing_law: MCL 287.1101 et seq. (Large Carnivore Act); NREPA Part 413, MCL 324.41301 et seq. (prohibited/restricted species).

breed.why: No Michigan statute requires a permit to breed pet rodents; the DNR captive-wildlife permit covers native game, not non-native rodents, and R. rattus is neither regulated game nor a prohibited invasive species. Breeding is unaddressed (effectively legal).
breed.governing_law: NREPA Part 413; Wildlife Conservation Order Ch. V (native game only).

sell_give.why: Michigan's Pet Shops Act (MCL 287.331+) requires a license to sell animals, but its definition of 'animal' EXCLUDES rodents — so a rodent-only seller isn't a regulated pet shop. Selling a prohibited invasive species would be unlawful, but R. rattus isn't on that list. No state breeder/dealer license reaches rodents.
sell_give.governing_law: MCL 287.331 et seq. (Pet Shops Act; rodents excluded); NREPA Part 413.

transport.why: Importing a non-native rodent requires an official interstate Certificate of Veterinary Inspection from a USDA-accredited vet; Michigan issues NO entry permit for non-native rodents (no permit number needed). Intrastate transport is unregulated. Never release a roof rat.
transport.governing_law: MDARD animal-movement requirements (Animal Industry Act); CVI by accredited vet.

restrictions.summary: Importing a non-native pet rodent into Michigan requires an interstate Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (MDARD); no Michigan entry permit. No CVI for in-state movement.
restrictions.where_to_file: Michigan Dept of Agriculture & Rural Development (MDARD), Animal Industry Division

restrictions.summary: Never release a roof rat. Local city/township/county ordinances may add limits — check yours.
